mainTopic: Where תפילין are worn: the source for the left arm, the left-handed person, the exact spots on arm and head, and the two-headed firstborn
overview: This amud continues the search for the source that תפילין של יד are worn on the left arm. רבי יוסי החורם shows that the right hand is also called יד, and the other תנא answers that plain יד still means the left. רבי נתן learns it another way: binding is done with the writing hand, the right, so the תפילין sit on the left. רב אשי learns it from the spelling יָדְכָה, read as 'the weak hand,' and defends this against רבי אבא's challenge. Two ברייתות then use the same word either for 'left' or to include a person missing an arm (גידם). A left-handed person (אטר) puts תפילין on his right arm, while one who uses both hands equally uses the regular left. The גמרא then fixes the exact spots: the bicep, and the top of the head where a baby's skull is soft. Finally, פלימו asks about a person with two heads. A real two-headed firstborn arrives, and an elder rules that the father pays ten סלעים, a ruling the גמרא begins to challenge, with the rest of the challenge coming on the next amud.

steps.title: The right hand is also called יד
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי החורם rejects the earlier proof by showing that the תורה calls the right hand יד too.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוסי החורם says: We have found the right hand called יד, as it says: 'And יוסף saw that his father placed his right hand.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוסי החורם pushes back against the earlier proof, which said that the plain word יד in the Torah means the left hand. He brings a פסוק where the right hand is called יד.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier proof depended on the idea that יד on its own always means the left hand. If the תורה ever calls the right hand יד, the word no longer points only to the left, and the proof falls apart.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei HaChorem says:
We have found the right hand being called 'yad,'
as it says: 'And Yosef saw
that his father was placing his right hand.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the earlier proof, given before this passage, that 'yad' means the left hand.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The claim that the plain word יד in the Torah refers only to the left hand.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: A פסוק in בראשית calls the right hand יד, so the word is not limited to the left.

steps.title: The other view: the right is never called plain יד
steps.stepSummary: The other תנא answers that the right hand is called 'his right hand,' never plain יד.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the other one? It is called 'his right hand'; it is not called plain יד.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks how the other תנא would answer רבי יוסי החורם's proof. It answers that in that פסוק the right hand is labeled with the extra word יְמִינוֹ, not with plain יד.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The original proof only claimed that יד with no extra word means the left. Since the פסוק about יוסף needed to add 'right' to make it the right hand, it actually fits the original claim.

keyTerms.meaning: And the other one (the other opinion)

phrases.english: And the other one?
phrases.notes: That's the תנא whose proof רבי יוסי החורם just rejected. How would he answer?

phrases.english: It is called 'his right hand,'
but it is not called plain 'yad.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Defends the earlier proof against רבי יוסי החורם's rejection.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the claim: only יד with no added word means the left hand.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since the right hand is called יד in בראשית, the word יד can mean either hand.
steps.terutzMaskana: The right hand needs the extra word יְמִינוֹ, so plain יד still means the left.

steps.title: רבי נתן: binding goes with writing
steps.stepSummary: רבי נתן derives that תפילין go on the left by linking binding (וּקְשַׁרְתָּם) to writing (וּכְתַבְתָּם).
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי נתן says: It is not needed, for it says 'And you shall bind them' and 'And you shall write them.' Just as writing is with the right hand, so too binding is with the right hand. And since binding is with the right hand, placing is on the left.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי נתן offers a whole new source for the rule. He links the two פסוקים that sit next to each other: binding the תפילין and writing the מזוזה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Most people write with the right hand, so binding must also be done with the right hand. You cannot tie something onto the same arm you are tying with, so the תפילין end up on the left arm.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not needed (there is no need for that proof)

steps.whatToRemember: According to רבי נתן, the right hand ties the תפילין, so they are worn on the left arm.

phrases.english: Rabbi Natan says: It is not needed,
for it says: 'And you shall bind them,' 'And you shall write them.'
Just as writing is done with the right hand,
so too binding is done with the right hand.
And since binding is with the right hand,
placing them is on the left.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different source that does not depend on the meaning of the word יד.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Binding is done with the right hand, like writing, so the תפילין are placed on the left arm.

steps.title: Where does רבי יוסי החורם learn 'left'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how רבי יוסי החורם knows that תפילין go on the left, since he rejected the יד proof.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יוסי החורם, placing on the left, from where does he know it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a question to set up the next step. רבי יוסי החורם knocked down one source, so it wants to know which source he uses.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nobody here argues that תפילין go on the left. The only question is which פסוק teaches it for someone who rejects the 'plain יד means left' proof.

keyTerms.meaning: From where does he know it?

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yosei HaChorem,
placing them on the left, from where does he know it?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבִּי יוֹסֵי הַחוֹרָם, הַנָּחָה דְּבִשְׂמֹאל מְנָא לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to רבי יוסי החורם after hearing רבי נתן's source.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which source רבי יוסי החורם uses for placing תפילין on the left.

steps.title: He uses רבי נתן's source
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי החורם learns it the same way as רבי נתן.
steps.simpleTranslation: He derives it from where רבי נתן derives it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that רבי יוסי החורם uses רבי נתן's source: binding goes with writing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This fills the gap left by step 1. רבי יוסי החורם does not need the word יד at all, because the link between binding and writing already gives him the left arm.

phrases.english: He derives it from where
Rabbi Natan derives it.

steps.triggerLanguage: נָפְקָא לֵיהּ מֵהֵיכָא דְּנָפְקָא לֵיהּ לְרַבִּי נָתָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 4.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רבי יוסי החורם uses רבי נתן's link between binding and writing.

steps.title: רב אשי: יָדְכָה with a ה means the weak hand
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי derives 'left' from the spelling יָדְכָה, read as יד כֵּהָה, the weak hand.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: From יָדְכָה, which is written with a ה: כֵּהָה, weak.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי gives a third source. The word for 'your hand' is spelled with an extra ה at the end, and he reads it as 'the weak hand,' which is the left.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The usual spelling is יָדְךָ. The longer spelling יָדְכָה ends with the sound כָּה, which רב אשי connects to כֵּהָה, meaning weak or dim. For most people the weaker hand is the left.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Your hand,' spelled with a ה at the end

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
It is learned from 'yadchah,' as it is written,
with a hei: 'keha,' the weak hand.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A third, independent source based on how the word is spelled.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The spelling יָדְכָה teaches that תפילין go on the weak hand, the left.

steps.title: רבי אבא: maybe it means the strong hand
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבא suggests reading the word as 'the hand of strength' (כֹּחַ), which would be the right.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבא said to רב אשי: But say 'your hand' that is of strength?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אבא challenges רב אשי. He asks why not read the ending as כֹּחַ, strength, which would point to the right hand.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The sound of כֹּחַ is close to כָּה, so a wordplay could go either way. If it can mean strong instead of weak, רב אשי's proof proves nothing, or even the opposite.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַבִּי אַבָּא לְרַב אָשֵׁי:
phrases.english: Rabbi Abba said to Rav Ashi:
But say it means 'your hand' that has strength?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רב אשי's reading.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב אשי's reading of יָדְכָה as כֵּהָה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ending could just as well be read as כֹּחַ, strength, which would point to the right hand.

steps.title: It is not spelled with a ח
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי answers that the word ends with ה, not ח, so it cannot mean כֹּחַ.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Is it written with a ח?
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי defends his reading. כֹּחַ ends with a ח, but the פסוק has a ה, so 'weak' is the reading that fits.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The reading has to follow the actual letters in the תורה. Since the letter is ה, which matches כֵּהָה, the 'strength' reading fails and רב אשי's source holds.

keyTerms.meaning: Is it written? (a question that expects 'no')

phrases.english: He said to him: Is it written with a ches?
phrases.notes: כֹּחַ would need a ח at the end, but the פסוק has a ה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבי אבא's challenge.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ending could mean כֹּחַ, the strong right hand.
steps.terutzMaskana: The word ends in ה, matching כֵּהָה, so it means the weak left hand.

steps.title: A dispute of תנאים about יָדְכָה
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא matches רב אשי, while אחרים use the same word to include a person missing part of his arm (גידם).
steps.simpleTranslation: Like a dispute of תנאים: יָדְכָה with a ה, this is the left. אחרים say: 'Your hand' comes to include the גידם.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that רב אשי's reading is the subject of a dispute between תנאים. The first view reads יָדְכָה as the left hand, like רב אשי. אחרים use the word to include a גידם in the מצוה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first תנא uses the extra ה to teach 'left,' exactly like רב אשי. אחרים use the word for a different law: a person whose arm is cut off still wears תפילין. So רב אשי follows one side of this dispute.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Others,' a תנא quoted without a name
A person whose arm is cut off

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think אחרים say תפילין go on the right. They use the word יָדְכָה to teach a different law, about the גידם.

phrases.english: This is like a dispute of tannaim:
'Yadchah' with a hei: this is the left.
Others say:
'Your hand' comes to include the gidem.
phrases.notes: Here the גידם is someone whose arm ends at the elbow. He still has to wear תפילין on what is left.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Places רב אשי's reading inside a dispute between תנאים.
steps.raayaObject: רב אשי's reading of יָדְכָה as the left hand.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא where the first תנא reads יָדְכָה with a ה as the left hand.

steps.title: Another ברייתא: one with no arm at all
steps.stepSummary: A second ברייתא says that someone with no arm is exempt from תפילין, while אחרים use יָדְכָה to include even him.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another ברייתא teaches: If he has no arm, he is exempt from תפילין. אחרים say: יָדְכָה comes to include the גידם.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second ברייתא with the same kind of dispute. The first view exempts a man with no left arm from תפילין. אחרים use יָדְכָה to obligate even him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the case is more extreme: there is no arm left at all, not even above the elbow. אחרים still include him, meaning he would wear the תפילין on his right arm.
steps.whatToRemember: The extra ה in יָדְכָה is used either for 'the left hand' (like רב אשי) or, by אחרים, to include a person missing an arm in the מצוה.

phrases.english: Another baraita teaches:

phrases.aramaic: אֵין לוֹ זְרוֹעַ – פָּטוּר מִן הַתְּפִילִּין,
phrases.english: If he has no arm, he is exempt from tefillin.
phrases.notes: He means no left arm at all, not even above the elbow.

phrases.english: Others say:
'Yadchah' comes to include the gidem.
phrases.notes: In this case he would put the תפילין on his right arm.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a second ברייתא with a parallel dispute about יָדְכָה.
steps.raayaObject: That יָדְכָה is used in a dispute between תנאים.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A second ברייתא about a person with no arm.

steps.title: A left-handed person puts תפילין on his right arm
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא rules that an אטר puts תפילין on his right arm, because for him that is the weaker arm.
steps.simpleTranslation: The חכמים taught: A left-handed person puts תפילין on his right arm, because for him that is the 'left' (weaker) arm.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא about where an אטר puts his תפילין של יד.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא's phrase 'which is his left' shows that 'left' here means the weaker hand, not the physical left side. So a left-handed person flips sides and uses his right arm.

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
A left-handed person puts tefillin on his right arm,
which is his 'left.'
phrases.notes: For him the right arm is the weaker one, so it counts as his 'left.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the source for 'left' to a practical case: where a left-handed person places his תפילין.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An אטר puts תפילין on his right arm, which is his weaker arm.

steps.title: Another ברייתא says he uses his left arm
steps.stepSummary: A second ברייתא says the אטר puts תפילין on his left arm, like everyone else.
steps.simpleTranslation: But it was taught: He puts them on his left arm, which is the left arm of every person!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the first ברייתא with another ברייתא that seems to say the opposite.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The second ברייתא follows the physical left side, which is the same for everyone. That clashes directly with the rule that an אטר uses his right arm.

keyTerms.meaning: The left arm of every person, meaning the ordinary physical left

phrases.english: But wasn't it taught:
He puts them on his left arm,
which is the left of every person!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Contradicts the ruling of step 11
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling that an אטר puts תפילין on his right arm
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Two ברייתות give opposite rulings for what looks like the same person.

steps.title: אביי: the second ברייתא is about someone who uses both hands
steps.stepSummary: אביי explains that the second ברייתא speaks about a person who uses both hands equally.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: When that ברייתא was taught, it was speaking about someone who controls both his hands.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי settles the contradiction by explaining that the two ברייתות are talking about two different people.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Someone who is fully left-handed puts תפילין on his right arm. Someone who uses both hands equally has no weaker hand, so he goes with the regular left arm like everyone else.

keyTerms.meaning: Controls both hands equally, meaning ambidextrous

steps.whatToRemember: A fully left-handed person uses his right arm. Someone who uses both hands equally uses his left arm.

phrases.english: Abaye said:
When that baraita was taught,
it was about one who controls both his hands.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in step 12
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases: each ברייתא speaks about a different person
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both ברייתות seemed to be about the same left-handed person.
steps.terutzMaskana: The second ברייתא is about a person who uses both hands equally, so he uses the regular left arm.

steps.title: The exact spots: the bicep and the top of the head
steps.stepSummary: דבי מנשה defines 'על ידך' as the bicep and 'בין עיניך' as the top of the head.
steps.simpleTranslation: דבי מנשה taught: 'On your arm' means the bicep. 'Between your eyes' means the top of the head.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new point: exactly where on the arm and head the תפילין go.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even though the פסוק says 'between your eyes,' the תפילין של ראש are not placed on the forehead between the eyes. They go higher, on the top of the head.

keyTerms.meaning: The bicep, the muscle of the upper arm

steps.confusionAlert: Do not read 'בין עיניך' literally as the spot between the eyes. The תפילין go up on the top of the head.

phrases.english: The school of Menashe taught:
'On your arm' — this is the bicep,
'Between your eyes' — this is the top of the head.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: New topic: the exact placement of both תפילין
steps.mimraCoreRuling: תפילין של יד go on the bicep. תפילין של ראש go on the top of the head.

steps.title: Where exactly on the top of the head?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the precise spot on the top of the head.
steps.simpleTranslation: Where?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a short follow-up question, setting up the next step's answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The top of the head is a fairly large area. The גמרא wants to know the exact spot within it.

phrases.english: Where?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for more detail about step 14
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The exact spot on the top of the head for the תפילין של ראש

steps.title: The soft spot on a baby's head
steps.stepSummary: דבי רבי ינאי say the תפילין של ראש go on the spot where a baby's skull is soft.
steps.simpleTranslation: דבי רבי ינאי say: The place where a baby's brain is soft.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question with a clear landmark: the soft spot on a newborn's head.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A newborn has a soft spot on the top of the skull. That same spot on an adult is where the תפילין של ראש are placed.
steps.whatToRemember: תפילין של ראש go on the top of the head, at the spot where a baby's skull is soft.

phrases.english: The school of Rabbi Yannai say:
The place where a baby's brain is soft.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 15
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The spot where a baby's skull is soft

steps.title: פלימו asks about a person with two heads
steps.stepSummary: פלימו asks רבי which head a two-headed person puts תפילין on.
steps.simpleTranslation: פלימו asked רבי: Someone who has two heads, on which of them does he put תפילין?
steps.whatsHappening: A new story begins. פלימו asks רבי an unusual question about תפילין.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now that we know the תפילין של ראש go on the top of the head, פלימו asks what happens if there are two heads. The question tests how far the rule stretches.

keyTerms.meaning: He asked him (put a question to him)

phrases.english: Peleimu asked Rabbi:
Someone who has two heads,
on which of them does he put tefillin?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the placement of the תפילין של ראש to ask about an extreme case
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which head a two-headed person puts תפילין on

steps.title: רבי rejects the question harshly
steps.stepSummary: רבי tells פלימו to either leave or accept a שמתא.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Either get up and go into exile, or accept a ban on yourself.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי refuses to answer and instead scolds פלימו for asking.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי does not give a ruling. He treats the question as mockery, not a real question. His words are a sharp rebuke.

keyTerms.meaning: Go into exile, leave this place
A ban, being pushed out of the community

phrases.english: He said to him:
Either get up and go into exile,
or accept a ban upon yourself.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the question of step 17
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: רבי treats the question as mocking and not worth answering.

steps.title: A real two-headed firstborn arrives
steps.stepSummary: A man arrives whose firstborn son has two heads and asks how much he must give the כהן for פדיון הבן.
steps.simpleTranslation: Meanwhile a certain man came and said to him: A baby with two heads was born to me. How much must I give to the כהן?
steps.whatsHappening: Right then a real case shows up. A man asks how much to pay for redeeming his two-headed firstborn.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Suddenly the 'silly' case of two heads is real, and it raises a practical money question about פדיון הבן. The question is whether this baby counts as one firstborn or two.

keyTerms.meaning: A כהן, who receives the redemption money for a firstborn

phrases.english: Meanwhile a certain man came,
and said to him:
A baby was born to me,
who has two heads.
How much must I give to the kohen?
phrases.notes: He is asking about redeeming his firstborn son, פדיון הבן.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A real two-headed case appears right after רבי rejected the question
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How much redemption money is owed for a two-headed firstborn

steps.title: An elder rules: ten סלעים
steps.stepSummary: An elder teaches that the father must give the כהן ten סלעים.
steps.simpleTranslation: A certain elder came and taught him: He must give him ten סלעים.
steps.whatsHappening: An elder answers the man's question with a clear amount.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The usual redemption payment is five סלעים. Ten means the baby is treated like two people for this payment.

phrases.english: A certain elder came and taught him:
He must give him ten sela coins.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the man's question in step 19
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Ten סלעים, double the usual amount

steps.title: Challenge from רמי בר חמא's teaching
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא questions the elder's ruling and begins quoting רמי בר חמא about a firstborn who is fatally injured within thirty days.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is that so? But רמי בר חמא teaches: Since it says 'You shall surely redeem the firstborn of man,' I might think that even if he was fatally injured within thirty days he must be redeemed. The פסוק teaches:
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the elder's ruling by starting to quote a teaching of רמי בר חמא. The quote continues past this point.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רמי בר חמא is about to limit the פסוק so that a baby who is fatally injured within thirty days is not redeemed. The challenge to the 'ten סלעים' ruling builds on that limit and is completed on the next amud.

keyTerms.meaning: Is that so? A challenge to what was just said

phrases.english: Is that so?
But Rami bar Chama teaches:
Since it is stated:
'You shall surely redeem the firstborn of man,'
